BAINAPI', reads (scanned letter-spacing removed): 'The twelve consonant phonemes seem to be p, t, k, b, d, g, m, n, s, l, w, and y. Bainapi has probably seven vowel phonemes: i, e, E, a, O, @, and u. The following vowel sequences have been observed: ei, ai, ia, ea, ae, au, ua, and au. It is well possible th…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey-level note only: stress exists at word level and is tentatively judged phonemic (i.e. not predictable by position), with vowel lengthening as its correlate; no default position, no examples or minimal pairs are given, and stress is not marked in the accompanying 170-item wordlist.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole statement is hedged ('seem', 'probably') and based on a short survey elicitation (Reesink's 1974-75 Aramia River survey).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from elicited citation forms in a survey wordlist; note that for neighbouring Kamula (p. 14) Reesink attributes observed vowel length to 'incidental heavy stress in repeating the word clearly for the investigator', so the Bainapi length-under-stress observation is of the same elicitation type.
new_statements.identity_note: Reesink 1976 describes the variety under the name Bainapi (informant's clan name), recorded at Pikiwa and identified by him with 'Dibiasu' of the Upper Bamu/Wawoi (Rentoul 1924) and 'Turumasa' as named at other villages; this is the same language as Glottolog dibi1240 Dibiyaso [dby] (alt. names Bainapi, Dibiasu, Pikiwa). No dialect differentiation is described.

No stress position rule, no stress marked in the wordlist.
